segments.en: Good to be with you.

Flash flood emergency, catastrophic flooding in New Mexico tonight, the high-water rescues happening as we come on the air.
The moment Jane Doe told Cornell University Police she was gang raped at that fraternity house, according to a transcript obtained exclusively by CBS New York.
So why was a criminal case not pursued?
Guilty, the former American Idol contestant Caleb Flynn convicted of aggravated murder for killing his wife.

And good evening.

We begin tonight with heavy rain across parts of the Southwest, putting nearly a third of the country at risk of flash floods in the hours ahead, the worst of it so far in New Mexico, where water has spilled over a 20-foot dam there, prompting emergency crews to warn those nearby, urging them to evacuate.
And in Arizona, more than 4 inches of rain has fallen in places, stranding some vehicles, sweeping others away entirely.
And the warnings tonight, things could get worse as the week goes on.
Meteorologist Rob Marciano with the latest.

ROB MARCIANO: Torrential rains triggering more flash flooding today in the Southwest, so much rain, the McLeod dam in Southern New Mexico is on the brink of failing, the National Weather Service issuing a rare flash flood emergency for areas downstream of the dam.
TOM HANSON: Going to be able to get the guy off the truck.
ROB MARCIANO: In Arizona, a dramatic rescue as a man stranded in floodwaters desperately clung to his truck.
It was one of more than 60 flash floods reported across the Southwest in the last 24 hours, leaving roads washed out and residents bracing for more.
I want to make sure I put some sandbags around where the rain starts creating where the water goes and starts creating sinkholes, and I'm just trying to prevent that.
ROB MARCIANO: The excess water being fed by Hurricane Polo as it came ashore today in Northern Mexico, driving inland with damaging winds and rainfall rates as high as 4 inches per hour.
That hurricane at one point a Category 5 storm.
So it's got a ton of moisture combining with yet another storm.
So we'll go through that, doesn't spell good news for this area, nor a good chunk of the country.
So we've got a flash flood warnings, over a dozen of them in effect right now across New Mexico and Arizona, even a severe thunderstorm warning in there as well, I-25 to I-10.
And then really, these flash flood watches extend over 1,200 miles.
Even the precip shield goes beyond Des Moines.
It will be in Chicago before you know it.
So here's how things will roll out.
The most intense rain for New Mexico will be tonight.
And then look at Dallas in the I-35 corridor tomorrow night into the early morning hours.
Those could be severe, and they will have an intense amount of rainfall as well.
Because now we have Polo, we got an upper-level low in the four corners tapping moisture from the Gulf, too, so 4 to 6 inches of rainfall.
It looks like it's going to be a very wet week ahead for a big chunk of the country.
Tony.
Rob, thank you very much.

We turn now to a CBS News exclusive, the new reporting tonight from our New York station, what a young woman at Cornell University told police two years ago about her alleged rape inside a frat house there and why no criminal charges were filed at the time.
Lilia Luciano continues her reporting tonight from Ithaca, New York.
LILIA LUCIANO: Tonight, new details nearly two years after a former Cornell University student says she was drugged and gang raped at a campus fraternity house.

According to a transcript obtained by CBS News New York, the woman, identified as Jane Doe, said during her interview with campus police three weeks after the alleged incident, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
None of the seven students she accused were criminally charged after the university said they conducted a thorough Title IX investigation.
We communicated to Cornell that we were willing to sit down with her.
She didn't get back to us.
LILIA LUCIANO: The DA says his office is now preparing the case for a grand jury.
A recently filed civil lawsuit by Jane Doe contains this screenshot of a group chat involving dozens of frat members.
They had this Snapchat post inviting men, 57 men, to participate in a gang rape.
They did nothing.
LILIA LUCIANO: The district attorney says Jane Doe's initial statement under oath described her drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.
Her attorney says she was traumatized, numb, and unable to function or accept the horror of what happened.
On the Cornell campus, students are demanding answers.
It's absolutely terrifying to hear that that's happening.
And then also that begs the question of, what if this happened to me?
What if this happened to my best friend?
What if this happened to someone and I didn't get my day in court and I have to go to a mass-media campaign just to be heard?
CBS News has reached out to the seven men named in the lawsuit.
We have only heard back from the attorneys of two of them.
They both deny the allegations.
Tony.
Lilia, thank you very much.

We turn now to breaking news out of Ohio, a guilty verdict in the murder trial of Caleb Flynn, the former music pastor and American Idol contestant, the jury siding with prosecutors, who said he killed his wife in an execution-style murder that he'd staged to look like a home invasion.
Ian Lee has details from court.
WOMAN: --find the defendant, Caleb C.
Flynn, guilty of aggravated murder.
IAN LEE: Caleb Flynn listened in stunned silence as the verdict was read, guilty on all counts, including murder, in the shooting death of his wife Ashley at their Tipp City, Ohio home in February.
The former American Idol contestant and pastor was charged with nine counts, ranging from evidence tampering to assault and murder, which carries the possibility of a life sentence.
You heard his statement three times with the police.
There wasn't any reason to put him on for a fourth time.
IAN LEE: The prosecution called 40 witnesses, including Flynn's one-time lover, 24-year-old Alleigha Botner.
She read aloud some of the more than 100,000 messages she said they exchanged.
At first it was, I want her dead.
I wish she was gone.
And then it was, if I could kill her and not go to jail, I would.
IAN LEE: Flynn was accused of shooting his wife twice while she was asleep in their bedroom.
The couple's daughters were home at the time, according to authorities.
They say Flynn attempted to cover up the killing by staging a burglary.
Flynn did not take the stand in his own defense.
During closing arguments today, his attorney says the prosecution did not have sufficient evidence.
The old gun was found.

That the prosecution had such strong evidence with those text messages, where you have a defendant literally saying, I want to or I wish I could kill my wife, and then no evidence to really undercut that.
Attorneys for Flynn plan to appeal.
Sentencing will take place here Monday afternoon.
Caleb Flynn faces the possibility of life in prison without parole.
Tony.
Ian, thank you very much.
Lindsay Clancy was back in court today, her first appearance since a mistrial earlier this month.
Prosecutors did not reveal their plans for a potential retrial.
But Clancy's attorney made a change today, arguing for the first time that there is no evidence Clancy killed her three small children, something he did not dispute in her first trial.
CBS News correspondent Shanelle Kaul has our update.
This entire case is based on speculation.
SHANELLE KAUL: In a case full of twists and turns, Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney delivered another shocker today.
Where does she say that she did this?
SHANELLE KAUL: Kevin Reddington, for the first time, suggesting prosecutors didn't prove Lindsay Clancy killed her children.
You have the woefully deficient fingerprinting.
You have the horrific, ridiculous investigation.
SHANELLE KAUL: The new argument even caught prosecutors off guard.
They fired back.
The first point that there isn't enough evidence to prove that she did it, I would suggest as a laughable argument.
I think this is a real shot across the bow for the Commonwealth to let them know that this is not going to be an easy trial for them.
SHANELLE KAUL: Prosecutors today stopped short of saying if they'll retry Clancy.
That's my goal in this thing, is to get this thing tried.
SHANELLE KAUL: But the judge told both sides to be ready to pick a new trial date at the next hearing on November 2.
The judge will also address several other motions that day, including one from Reddington.
My name is Michael Peguy Desronvil, also known as the lone juror.
SHANELLE KAUL: Asking for the holdout juror to be investigated.
Today his attorney defended him.
Jurors should not have to worry about coming in and having them outed because they take a stance different than everyone else.

If prosecutors decide to retry this case on lesser charges, manslaughter or second-degree murder, Lindsay Clancy could waive her right to a jury trial, meaning a judge could ultimately be responsible for deciding her fate instead of 12 jurors.
Tony.
Shanelle, thank you.
President Trump has been saying he sees no need for the government to rein in or slow down artificial intelligence.
And after meeting with a group of major tech leaders today, he is sticking with that position.
Here's CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
These are the most brilliant people in the world.
NANCY CORDES: In an extraordinary meeting at the White House, many of the nation's most powerful AI leaders urged President Trump to let them police themselves.
He agreed.
There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation.
NANCY CORDES: Surrounding Trump were the heads of Meta, Google, NVIDIA, SpaceX, Amazon, and OpenAI.
Just this week, OpenAI announced it is pausing the release of its newest AI model over safety concerns.
Reuters reported that Anthropic, whose CEO was there today too, plans to caution potential investors that AI could pose, quote, "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."
Alex Karp is the CEO of Palantir.
Do you think the president's mind changed in any way when it comes to the dangers associated with AI?
You should ask the president.
How would I know that?
NANCY CORDES: The data center controversy came up, too, with Trump urging the CEOs to build goodwill by supplying more electricity and school funding to local communities.
The people in those areas-- we discussed this at length today-- they're going to greatly benefit financially.
REPORTER 1: Do you want them to stay away from homes when they're building these data centers?
Yeah, I think I want them to be in the right location within a community.
REPORTER 2: Mr. President-- There are tech executives who support more government guardrails for AI, but they held back today, at least when the cameras were on.
The leaders did sign a commitment here to build strong internal controls.
Trump called the document, quote, "morally binding."
Tony.
Very interesting, Nancy.
Thank you.

We have an update tonight on a story we reported last week, more than 100 people claiming that they suffered brain injuries from riding the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California.
The theme park says that ride is now permanently closed because of a drop in what it calls guest confidence.
Lawsuits against Six Flags are still moving forward.

And British authorities are defending their decision to let a group of young men go free, even as investigators look into a suspected terror plot near an air base there used by the US military to attack Iran.
CBS's Ramy Inocencio reports tonight from London.
Yes, Tony, the head of the UK's counterterrorism police confirmed that no explosive devices were found in the three vans discovered near RAF Fairford but did say a quantity of gasoline was recovered.
Now, five men, all British citizens in their 20s, were arrested early Sunday morning on suspicion of preparing a terror attack.
Police released all five of them on bail Monday, prompting criticism from President Trump, who said he was disappointed in calling those men terrorists.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said that what happened over the weekend clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor.
The speculation there has been Iran, which the embassy here has categorically rejected.
British police again today emphasized the men are still under investigation as they continue to probe what the men were doing near that base and if a foreign government was involved.
Tony.
Ramy, thank you very much.

In other news, if you doubt that today's younger generation can step up in a moment of crisis, we have a story for you out of Central Pennsylvania, featuring a group of high school kids and an out-of-control school bus.
Here's CBS's Tom Hanson.
TOM HANSON: The school bus' security camera captured what began as a routine stop for these students in Central Pennsylvania.
Can I get off?
TOM HANSON: But as kids waited at the door, the bus started to move.
A group of quick-thinking students jumped into action after they noticed the bus driver limp over the steering wheel, foot still on the gas pedal.
But within seconds, sophomore Alexis Smith and senior Skyla Horton forced the bus to brake.
I went up front and went behind Alexis, and then she put her full force onto the brakes.
So I fell.
Brake, brake brake.
And then I jumped back up and pulled the parking brake, so nothing further could happen.
TOM HANSON: Smith then called for help over the bus's radio.
Our bus driver just passed out.
TOM HANSON: And checked the pulse of the driver.
None of the passengers were hurt.
I knew that he needed medical attention, so that's why I just jumped into helping him.
TOM HANSON: The students' heroics big news at school, the driver grateful.
ALEXIS SMITH: He said thank you.
That was the first thing he said to me.
And I said, you're welcome.
And that bus driver is back to work.
The students credit their health science class for teaching them first aid.
Tony.
Tom, thank you very much.
Still ahead on the broadcast tonight, the rising cost of airfare, what to know about when to book to get the best deals on holiday travel.
Stay with us.
Flying this holiday season is going to cost you a whole lot more, but there are ways to save.
Senior transportation correspondent Kris Van Cleave explains.
KRIS VAN CLEAVE: Coming to the nation's airports this fall, a nonstop flight to holiday travel sticker shock.
I just anticipate the cost being close to $1,000 and then just picking up extra work to make that.

KRIS VAN CLEAVE: Airfare tracker Hopper's holiday travel index predicts 2026 will be the most expensive holiday travel season in a decade, driven primarily by rising jet fuel prices due to the conflict with Iran.
Hopper says the average domestic round trip for Thanksgiving will hit $402, up 31% from 2025.
Christmas time will cost you even more, on average $452, up 23% from last year.
I would absolutely recommend that travelers book their Thanksgiving and Christmas travel before Halloween.
The sweet spot is the next two weeks or so.
KRIS VAN CLEAVE: Amid those higher fuel prices, Alaska Airlines is debuting its fancy, new business-class suites and new premium economy options.
CEO Ben Minicucci says it's following customer demand, but rising fares are squeezing some.
Is the idea of that low-fare flight deal gone?
Can it exist at $4-plus a gallon fuel.
I think it gets more difficult.
Are there people that aren't taking trips now?
The strongest demand we're seeing is in premium and less in main cabin.
So that's an area that we're focused on, is how do we get people that are not going on that trip because of the increase in fares.
Still, Minicucci says holiday demand looks strong.
So don't expect there to be a fare sale close to the holidays.
He says, it's just not going to happen this year.
So book early, be flexible.
Avoid the Sunday after Thanksgiving if you can.
Hopper says simply traveling back Monday or Tuesday could save you $250 a ticket.
And if you're sitting on a bunch of points, this might be the year to use them for the holidays.
Tony.
Kris, good advice.
Appreciate it.
Coming up after the break, the car crash and the rescue that came just in time.
A group of fifth graders was injured this morning when their school bus crashed in Indianapolis.
It collided with a state police pickup truck, then rolled onto its side.
Fortunately, no life-threatening injuries to the kids, and the troopers are also in stable condition.
An auto body shop in Dallas got an extreme customer this week when a driver lost control and slammed into the shop's wall.
Two people then ran into dragged the driver out just as the car burst into flames, and then everyone took off before police arrived for one reason or another.
They didn't even wait for their estimate.
Time now for Fat Bear 2026.
Voting ends tonight between these finalists and what's been described as a battle of size, skill, snack acquisition, and strategic loafing, all of it in Alaska's Katmai National Park.
Bear 910 is the daughter of a previous champ-- there she is-- while Bear 89, a.k.a. Backpack, is a 20-year-old male returning from a serious leg injury.
Final results back here tomorrow night.
Still ahead, The Good Stuff and the strangers who stepped up to save this couple's dream wedding.
We are back with The Good Stuff tonight, a wedding story for the ages.
Kimberly Laprad and her husband to be, Jayden Sink, had saved up for a destination wedding on North Carolina's Hatteras Island last Friday.
But then the island got hammered by last week's storm, cutting off travel so badly, all but six of their guests got stuck on the mainland.
But while the couple was cut off from friends and family, they were not alone.
They put out a call on social media, inviting everyone on the island to a wedding.

And it feels like everyone on the island responded, including a DJ, a photographer, a caterer, a decorator, a beautiful venue owner, and even an officiant for what turned into maybe the island's best wedding party of the year.
I've never seen anything like it.
We could never have done anything like this back in our hometown.
Everybody here, they're just so selfless.
They don't care.
They're just willing to give, give, give, and don't really expect anything back either.
Kimberly and Jayden, congrats to you.
You've been married for less than a week, and you've already weathered the storm.
That's another day in America.
I'm Tony Dokoupil.
For all of us here at CBS News, thank you for watching tonight.
We'll see you right back here tomorrow.
Good night.
Take me back to my.
